proof.text: First, every $a\in B\setminus P$ is a nonzerodivisor and divides a positive power of $\varphi$. Choose $n\geq1$ with $a\notin\varphi^nB$. By hypothesis $(a,\varphi^n)=dB$ for a nonzerodivisor $d$. Write $a=du$, $\varphi^n=dv$, and $d=ra+s\varphi^n$. Cancellation of $d$ gives $1=ru+sv$, so one of $u,v$ is a unit, since $B$ is local. The alternative that $v$ is a unit would give $a\in\varphi^nB$. Thus $u$ is a unit; consequently $a$ is a nonzerodivisor and $\varphi^n=a(u^{-1}v)$.

source.place: XX 4.4, printed pp.373–374, the paragraph beginning Say I=(phi); explicit local algebra filling in the sketch.

proof.text: The ideal $P$ contains no power $\varphi^r$, even for $r=0$: membership would give $\varphi^r=\varphi^{r+1}b$, hence $1=\varphi b$ by regularity, contradicting that $\varphi$ is a nonunit. If $a,b\notin P$, Step 1 gives $\varphi^r=ac$ and $\varphi^s=be$. Thus $ab\in P$ would imply $\varphi^{r+s}=abce\in P$, a contradiction. Hence $P$ is a proper prime ideal. In particular $V=B/P$ is a domain and the image $\bar\varphi$ is nonzero. Since $P\subseteq\varphi B\subseteq\mathfrak m_B$, the quotient is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_B/P$, and $\bar\varphi$ remains a nonunit.

source.place: XX 4.4, printed pp.373–374, the paragraph beginning Say I=(phi); explicit local algebra filling in the sketch.

proof.text: For every $a\notin P$ one has $P=aP$. Indeed, choose $r$ and $e$ with $\varphi^r=ae$. Given $p\in P$, write $p=\varphi^r b= a(eb)$ and put $q=eb$. For each $n\geq1$, also write $p=\varphi^{r+n}b_n=a(e\varphi^n b_n)$. Since $a$ is a nonzerodivisor, $q=e\varphi^n b_n\in\varphi^nB$. Thus $q\in P$, proving $P\subseteq aP$; the reverse inclusion is the ideal property. In particular $P=\varphi P$ and $P=d^2P$ for every $d\notin P$.

source.place: XX 4.4, printed pp.373–374, the paragraph beginning Say I=(phi); explicit local algebra filling in the sketch.

proof.text: Regularity of $\varphi$ makes $B\to S$ injective, so regard $B$ as a subring of $S$. Step 3 gives $PS=P$ as subsets of $S$, because $p/\varphi^k\in P$ for $p\in P$. An element $b/\varphi^k$ with $b\notin P$ is invertible in $S$ by Step 1. An element with $b\in P$ cannot be invertible: an inverse $c/\varphi^l$ would give $bc=\varphi^{k+l}$ in $B$, contrary to Step 2. The nonunits of $S$ therefore form exactly the proper ideal $PS$, proving that $S$ is local with maximal ideal $PS$ and $PS\cap B=P$.

source.place: XX 4.4, printed pp.373–374, the paragraph beginning Say I=(phi); explicit local algebra filling in the sketch.

proof.text: For any nonzero $\bar a,\bar b\in V$, choose lifts $a,b\notin P$. Step 1 supplies a power $\varphi^n\in aB$, so $(a,b)$ is one of the ideals in the hypothesis. Write $(a,b)=dB$, $a=du$, $b=dv$, with $d$ a nonzerodivisor. Since $d\in(a,b)$, cancellation gives $1=ru+sv$ for some $r,s\in B$. At least one of $u,v$ is a unit; hence $a$ divides $b$ or $b$ divides $a$. Reducing modulo $P$ gives the same divisibility alternative in $V$. Every nonzero fraction $\bar a/\bar b$ or its inverse therefore belongs to $V$, which is exactly the valuation-ring condition [def-trf-valuation-ring].

source.place: XX 4.4, printed pp.373–374, the paragraph beginning Say I=(phi); explicit local algebra filling in the sketch.

proof.text: The surjective homomorphism $S\to V[1/\bar\varphi]$, $b/\varphi^k\mapsto\bar b/\bar\varphi^k$, has kernel $PS$: a fraction maps to zero precisely when $\bar\varphi^l\bar b=0$ for some $l$, and the domain $V$ with $\bar\varphi\ne0$ makes this equivalent to $b\in P$. It therefore identifies $S/PS$ with $V[1/\bar\varphi]$. Every nonzero $\bar b\in V$ divides a power of $\bar\varphi$ by Step 1, so it becomes invertible in this localization. Thus this localization is a field containing $V$, and is its fraction field by the fraction formulas. All the identifications are induced by the canonical quotient map.

source.place: XX 4.4, printed pp.373–374, the paragraph beginning Say I=(phi); explicit local algebra filling in the sketch.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-integral-over-henselian-pair] to $(B,\mathfrak m_B)$ and the quotient homomorphism $B\to V$. The pair is henselian by the hypothesis on $B$; the quotient map is integral since each image of $b$ satisfies the monic polynomial $T-b$. The cited statement makes $(V,\mathfrak m_BV)$ henselian. By Step 2, $\mathfrak m_BV=\mathfrak m_V$, so $V$ is henselian local as required.

source.place: Tag 09XK, lemma-integral-over-henselian-pair; applied to the quotient by P.

proof.text: To establish henselianity of $S$, take a monic $F\in S[X]$ and a simple root $\alpha$ of its reduction in $S/PS$. Choose $a\in S$ lifting $\alpha$ and write $a=b/\varphi^k$ with $b\in B$, $k\geq0$. Choose $l\geq k$ large enough to clear the finitely many coefficient denominators in $G(X)=\varphi^lF(X/\varphi^k)$, so $G\in B[X]$. Then $G(b)\in PS\cap B=P$ and $d=G'(b)=\varphi^{l-k}F'(a)\in B$ is a unit in $S$, since $F'(a)$ has nonzero image in the residue field of the local ring $S$. Hence $d\notin P$. By Step 3 choose $c\in P$ with $G(b)=d^2c$.

source.place: XX 4.4, printed pp.373–374, the paragraph beginning Say I=(phi); explicit local algebra filling in the sketch.

proof.text:
Expand $G(b+Y)=d^2c+dY+\sum_{i=2}^N g_iY^i$, choosing $N\geq\max(2,\deg G)$ and padding with zero coefficients. Set $h_i=g_i d^{i-2}$, $H(T)=c+T+\sum_{i=2}^N h_iT^i$, and form the monic polynomial
$$Q(Z)=Z^N+Z^{N-1}+\sum_{i=2}^N h_i c^{i-1}Z^{N-i}\in B[Z].$$
Since $c\in P\subseteq\mathfrak m_B$, its reduction is $Z^{N-1}(Z+1)$, whose root $-1$ is simple: the derivative there is $(-1)^{N-1}\ne0$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-henselian-local-root-lifting] to the henselian local ring $B$ and this monic $Q$. Obtain $z\in B$ with $Q(z)=0$ and $z\equiv-1\pmod{\mathfrak m_B}$, so $z$ is a unit. Put $t=c/z\in P$. Direct substitution gives $H(t)=cz^{-N}Q(z)=0$, and the displayed expansion gives $G(b+dt)=d^2H(t)=0$. Thus $a+dt/\varphi^k$ is a root of $F$ congruent to $a$ modulo $PS$. Every simple root of a monic polynomial over $S/PS$ lifts in this way. The reverse implication of [lem-weil-pbc-henselian-local-root-lifting], now for the local ring $S$ of Step 4, proves that $S$ is henselian.

source.place: Tag 04GF, definition-henselian, and Tag 04GG, lemma-characterize-henselian, via the cited monic-root criterion; agent-written reciprocal-polynomial calculation filling ILO XX 4.4, printed p.373.

proof.text: Finally use the additive valuation $v:K^\times\to\Gamma=K^\times/V^\times$ associated with the valuation ring $V$ [def-trf-valuation-ring], with order specified by $v(x)\geq v(y)$ exactly when $x/y\in V$, and $v(0)=+\infty$. Put $\delta=v(\bar\varphi)>0$, using Step 2. For $\gamma\in\Gamma$, choose $x\in K^\times$ with $v(x)=\gamma$. If $\gamma\geq0$, then $x\in V\setminus\{0\}$ and Step 1, applied to a lift of $x$, gives $\bar\varphi^r\in xV$. Hence $r\delta\geq\gamma$ and $(r+1)\delta>\gamma$. If $\gamma<0$, already $\delta>\gamma$. Thus the positive multiples of $\delta$ are cofinal in $\Gamma$. Each $\bar\varphi^nV=\{x:v(x)\geq n\delta\}$ contains the open ball $\{x:v(x)>n\delta\}$, so is a neighbourhood of zero. Conversely, for each ball $\{x:v(x)>\gamma\}$ choose $n\geq1$ with $n\delta>\gamma$; then $\bar\varphi^nV$ is contained in that ball. This proves precisely the asserted neighbourhood-basis and topology claim.

title: Henselian localization and valuation quotient of an I-valuative local ring
statement:
Let $B$ be a nonzero commutative henselian local ring [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], and let $\varphi\in B$ be a nonunit nonzerodivisor. Assume that every finitely generated ideal of $B$ containing $(\varphi^n)$ for some $n\geq1$ is principal and generated by a nonzerodivisor. Put $P=\bigcap_{n\geq1}\varphi^nB$, $S=B[1/\varphi]$, and $V=B/P$. Then $P$ is prime, $S$ is a henselian local ring with maximal ideal $PS$, and $V$ is a henselian valuation ring [def-trf-valuation-ring]. The canonical quotient map identifies
$$S/PS=V[1/\bar\varphi]=\operatorname{Frac}(V),$$
where $\bar\varphi$ is the image of $\varphi$ in $V$ and $\operatorname{Frac}(V)$ is its fraction field. Moreover $\bar\varphi$ is nonzero and noninvertible, and the ideals $\bar\varphi^nV$ form a neighbourhood basis of zero for the valuation topology, whose neighbourhoods are the sets $\{x:v(x)>\gamma\}$ for the additive valuation associated with $V$.
